planting.note: Grow in shallow pots or mounted, or as a groundcover in zone 10-11 shade; Foster's Vriesea has no frost tolerance and is damaged below 35°F. Keep the central cup filled with fresh water and flush periodically to prevent stagnation.

directions: Give bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun in a well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix or shallow pot. Foster's Vriesea forms a broad, arching rosette of wide, glossy leaves banded crosswise in alternating dark green and lighter silvery-green to purplish stripes, a bold horizontal pattern that makes it a striking specimen even without bloom. Once mature, it sends up a tall, flattened, sword-shaped flower spike in bright red to orange bearing small yellow flowers, a long-lasting display that can persist for weeks. Like other tank bromeliads it holds water in its central cup, which should be kept filled with fresh water and flushed periodically to prevent stagnation, and after flowering the parent rosette slowly declines while producing offset pups that can be separated once well rooted.

planting.note: Plant offsets in very well-drained, gritty, sandy soil in full sun; unlike most bromeliads, Dyckia is a terrestrial, drought-tolerant, rock-garden species that wants dry conditions between waterings rather than a water-filled central cup.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, sandy soil in full sun. Unlike the tank-forming, water-holding bromeliads most people picture, Dyckia platyphylla is a terrestrial, rock-garden succulent bromeliad with broad, stiff, silvery-green leaves edged in sharp, backward-curving spines, forming a dense, architectural rosette suited to xeriscape and rock garden plantings rather than shade. Established clumps send up tall, wiry flower spikes bearing small orange to yellow flowers in spring, drawing hummingbirds and pollinators. It tolerates drought, poor soil, and heat with ease once established, needing only sharp drainage, and slowly forms an expanding colony of offsets around the base that can be divided to start new plantings. Handle with care, since the sharp marginal spines can scratch.

planting.note: Grow in shallow pots or mounted, or as a groundcover in zone 10-11 partial shade; Aechmea recurvata has no frost tolerance and is damaged below 35°F. Keep the central cup filled with fresh water and flush periodically to prevent stagnation.

directions: Give bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun in a well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix or shallow pot. Aechmea recurvata is a compact species with narrow, arching, slightly toothed leaves that flush red toward the base as the plant approaches bloom, forming a small, tidy rosette well suited to a windowsill or small mixed bromeliad planting rather than a large specimen display. A compact flower head of small violet-blue flowers surrounded by bright pink to red bracts rises from the cup, providing long-lasting color. Like other tank bromeliads it holds water in its central cup, which should be kept filled with fresh water and flushed periodically to prevent stagnation, and after flowering the parent rosette slowly declines while producing offset pups that can be separated once well rooted.
